title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
6.5 Packages
We have so far used only base R: the functions that ship with R itself. R’s true reach comes from packages. A package is a collection of functions, datasets, and documentation, packaged together by the people who developed it. Packages let people who are not part of the R core team contribute new functions to the ecosystem and let any user benefit from those contributions.
Some packages come from the R core team and are maintained alongside R itself. The vast majority come from researchers, practitioners, and hobbyists who needed a particular tool, wrote it, documented it, and made it available. The total number of packages on the central R archive (CRAN) is in the tens of thousands and grows continuously.
A useful default attitude: when you have a task and you are about to write the code yourself, search first to see whether someone has already written a package for it. They usually have.

6.5.1 Installing and loading
Two distinct steps are involved in using a package: installing it (downloading it from the internet onto your computer) and loading it (telling the current R session to make its functions available).
You install a package once per computer. The standard command:

install.packages("psych")

This downloads and installs the package called psych. The quotation marks are required. After installation, the package sits on your hard drive but is not yet active in your session.
You load a package every session in which you want to use it:

library(psych)

After this line, all the functions in psych are available in the current session, just as if they were part of base R. If you restart R (which, recall from Chapter 4, you should do regularly), you will need to call library(psych) again before the package’s functions are available.
A common confusion: install.packages() requires quotes around the package name; library() does not. This is an inconsistency in R’s history; you simply have to remember it.


6.5.2 Finding documentation
After loading a package, you can read its documentation in three ways.
Help on a single function. Use ? followed by the function name:

?describe

This opens the help page for describe() in the Help panel of RStudio.
Help on the package as a whole. Each well-maintained package has an overview page:

help(package = "psych")

This lists every function in the package, with a one-line description.
Vignettes. Many packages include longer narrative tutorials, called vignettes, written by the authors. To list the vignettes in a package:

vignette(package = "psych")

To open one:

vignette("intro", package = "psych")

Vignettes are often the best resource when learning a new package, because they show how the functions are intended to be used together.


6.5.3 A worked example: psych::describe() and describeBy()
Let us work through a concrete example using psych, a package widely used in psychology and the social sciences.

install.packages("psych")  # only if you have not installed it already
library(psych)

The function describe() produces a more thorough version of summary(). On a numeric vector or a data frame, it returns the number of valid cases, the mean, the standard deviation, the median, the minimum, the maximum, the range, the skewness, the kurtosis, and the standard error of the mean.

describe(survey$age)
# returns a one-row table with the columns above
describe(survey)
# returns one row per numeric column

For a researcher working with social and behavioral data, the additional columns (skewness, kurtosis, standard error) are often exactly what you want.
describeBy() does the same, but separately for each level of a grouping variable. Suppose you also have a condition variable:

survey$condition <- c("control", "treatment", "control", "treatment", "control")
describeBy(survey$item1, group = survey$condition)
# returns a separate describe table for control and treatment

This is a one-line operation that, in SPSS, would be a multi-step menu walk through “Split File” and then “Descriptives.”


6.5.4 An alternative without library()
There is a second way to use a package’s functions without loading it into the session: the double-colon operator ::. The syntax is package::function:

psych::describe(survey$age)

This calls describe() from the psych package without having loaded psych. The package must still be installed; it just does not have to be loaded.
This style has two advantages and one cost.
The advantages: it makes the source of every function explicit (a reader can tell at a glance which package each function comes from), and it avoids problems caused by two packages defining a function with the same name (because psych::describe and Hmisc::describe, both real, are unambiguous when written with ::).
The cost: it is more verbose. Code that uses the same function many times becomes cluttered.
A reasonable convention: use library() for packages whose functions you will call frequently in a script, and use package::function style for one-off calls to functions from packages you do not otherwise need.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
6.6 Summary
The chapter has covered four threads, each of which will recur throughout the rest of the book.
Basic operations are the day-to-day vocabulary of working in R. You assign a value to a name with the arrow <-. You combine values with the standard arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, ^, plus modulo and integer division), and these operators work element-wise on vectors as naturally as they work on single numbers. You summarize a vector with mean, sd, median, min, max, sum, length, var, and the catch-all summary. You will see all of these constantly. The single non-obvious detail is that most summary functions return NA when the input contains any NA; setting na.rm = TRUE computes the summary over the non-missing values, and you will type that argument many times in real data analysis.
Custom functions were introduced for illustration. You saw the basic structure (name <- function(arguments) { body }), a small example with if and else for input checking, and the way a custom function can be called like any other. The point at this stage is to recognize the structure when you read code written by others, not to write your own. We will return to writing functions much later in the book, once using existing functions is comfortable.
The substantive example with the distorted survey was the centerpiece of the chapter. The same correction was applied to ten variables in three increasingly compact ways: ten manual assignments, ten function calls, and a single line that applies the function to all ten columns at once. The progression illustrates the three benefits coding has over click-based tools. The correction formula lives in one place, so a fix is one edit rather than ten. The code does not grow with the number of variables, so a sixty-variable dataset uses the same two working lines as a ten-variable one. And the intent is more legible than ten or sixty repeated lines. None of those benefits is available in SPSS or Excel. This is the most concrete answer the book offers to the question of why one would learn to code at all.
Packages are how the R ecosystem extends itself. A package is a collection of functions, datasets, and documentation contributed by someone (the R core team, or a researcher, or a hobbyist) and made available for anyone to install and use. The two-step install-then-load distinction matters: install.packages("name") runs once per computer, library(name) runs every R session in which you want the package’s functions to be available. You can read documentation through ?function_name, through help(package = "name") for an overview of everything in a package, or through vignette() for the longer narrative tutorials some packages include. You can also avoid loading a package entirely by writing package::function(), which is useful for one-off calls and for disambiguating functions that have the same name in different packages.
You now have the conceptual foundations of working in R. Chapter 7 is a brief recap, and after that you are ready for the rest of the book.

title: 6  Basic operations, custom functions, and packages
text:
6.7 Check your understanding
1. What is the difference between <- and = for assignment in R?

 x = 5 is the only correct way to assign in R; x <- 5 is wrong. Both work, but <- is the convention in R; = has another meaning inside function calls (named arguments). <- and = are completely interchangeable; there is no difference. <- only works inside functions, not in scripts.

2. What does mean() return when applied to a vector containing one or more NA values, by default?

 mean() returns 0 by default. mean() returns NA by default; setting na.rm = TRUE computes the mean of the non-missing values. mean() automatically removes missing values without needing any argument. R refuses to run mean() on a vector containing NA.

3. Which is the correct syntax for defining a function named quick_summary that takes one argument x?

 function quick_summary(x) { ... } quick_summary <- function(x) { ... } define quick_summary(x) { ... } quick_summary = function: x -> { ... }

4. What is the main advantage of applying a custom function to all relevant variables at once, compared to applying it manually one variable at a time?

 It is faster than the manual approach but produces different results. It scales to many more variables without growing in length, makes the correction formula live in one place, and keeps the intent of the code clear. It is the only way to apply a correction to a data frame. It avoids the need to ever inspect the data.

5. What does install.packages("psych") do?

 It downloads but does not install the package. It loads an already-installed package into the current session. It downloads and installs a package on your computer; this needs to be done once per computer. It is required at the start of every R session for every package.

6. How often do you need to call library(psych)?

 Once: it persists across all future sessions. It loads automatically; no library() call is ever needed. At the start of every R session in which you want to use the package's functions. Only when the package is installed.

7. What is the :: operator used for, as in psych::describe()?

 It is a way to install a package directly from a function call. It calls a function from a package without loading the entire package into the session. It is the only way to call functions from packages developed by others. It tells R to ignore the package and use a base R version of the function instead.

8. Which of the following best describes describe() from the psych package?

 It is faster than summary() but returns less information. It is a base R function, available without loading any package. It is in the psych package and returns a richer set of descriptive statistics than base R's summary(), including skewness, kurtosis, and the standard error of the mean. It only works on data frames, not on vectors.

title: 7  Recap and getting data into R
text:
7.1 Where you are now
The previous six chapters introduced R from the ground up. You have not yet analyzed any real data, and that is intentional: most of the difficulty new users encounter with R is not statistical but environmental. People struggle not because regression is hard but because they cannot tell the difference between an R script and an R project, or because they do not know that an R session has been silently inheriting state from yesterday. By the end of Section 1, those obstacles are behind you.
This chapter has three purposes. The first is to recap the six earlier chapters in compact form. The second is to introduce one practical step that Section 1 has not yet covered: how to load data from a file into R. The third is to point you toward what comes next. The questions at the end consolidate concepts across all six earlier chapters and the new material on data import.

title: 7  Recap and getting data into R
text:
7.2 What you have learned
Chapter 1 introduced R and the case for working with code. R is a free, open-source programming language designed for statistics. The reasons to use it rather than SPSS or Excel are reproducibility (the script is a complete record of what you did), error detection (every step is inspectable), and scaling (operations defined once can be applied to many variables). R is “object-based” in the sense that almost everything you work with is a named object, created by you, that can be passed into functions to produce new objects.
Chapter 2 distinguished R the engine from RStudio the dashboard. R performs the computations; RStudio provides the working environment around it. You install both, and the standard environment for new users is RStudio Desktop (Open Source Edition). Alternatives exist (Positron, VS Code with the R extension, Jupyter), but RStudio remains the easiest entry point.
Chapter 3 mapped out the relevant kinds of files and one in-memory state. The environment holds your objects while R is running and disappears when R closes. An R script (.R) is a saved record of code. An RData file (.RData) is a saved snapshot of objects. An R project (.Rproj) is a folder formally designated as a project, which sets the working directory and groups related files. R Markdown (.Rmd) files mix prose and code to produce finished documents. The script is the authoritative record; everything else is for convenience or for reporting.
Chapter 4 examined R sessions and how they relate to projects. A session is one running instance of R; opening a project starts a session, closing or restarting the session destroys the in-memory state. The recommended habit is to restart the session frequently and re-run the script from the top, so that no object exists in the environment for reasons other than your script. The corresponding RStudio settings (“Restore .RData into workspace at startup” and “Save workspace to .RData on exit”) should be turned off, because they silently preserve state across sessions in a way that obscures bugs.
Chapter 5 introduced the main object types: single values (numbers, strings, logicals), vectors (ordered sequences of values of the same type), and data frames (rows are observations, columns are variables, each column a vector). It introduced the indexing rules, including 1-based indexing, the $ for column extraction, and the [rows, columns] two-dimensional bracket form. It also introduced functions: pieces of R that take objects as input and return objects as output, with a small toolkit (class, length, str, head, summary, nrow, ncol, colnames) that you will use to inspect almost any unfamiliar object.
Chapter 6 covered the basic operations of arithmetic and summary statistics, gave a first illustration of writing a custom function (with if and else), and worked through a substantive example in which a survey dataset with many distorted variables was corrected three ways: manually, with a function applied repeatedly, and with a function applied to all variables in one line. The third approach is the one that pays off in practice. The chapter ended with packages: how to install them, how to load them, how to find documentation, with psych::describe() and psych::describeBy() as concrete examples, and the :: notation as an alternative to loading.

7.3 What this means for the rest of the book
You now have everything you need to start using R for actual data analysis. The remaining sections of the book will introduce specific kinds of analysis and operations relevant to the 4 other pillars (data visualization, statistical modeling, statistical inference, causal inference) in combination with R coding (i.e., the 5th pillar), and the corresponding R workflow for each. Where Section 1 was about setting up the environment, the remaining sections will be about doing things with it.
Two pieces of advice for the transition.
The first is that you should expect to consult the help system constantly. Even researchers with decades of R experience read help pages routinely. The skill that distinguishes someone fluent in R is not memorizing every function but knowing how to find the right one.
The second is that the workflow you have learned (project, restart, script, save explicitly when needed) is more important than any specific analysis you will run later. Statistical operations come and go; methods evolve; specific R functions are sometimes superseded by better ones. The discipline of organizing a project, restarting cleanly, and writing a script that reproduces an analysis from start to finish will serve you regardless of which analyses you eventually run.

title: 7  Recap and getting data into R
section: 7.4 A final missing piece: getting data into R
text:
7.4 A final missing piece: getting data into R
There is one practical step we have not yet covered. You know how to create objects from scratch, but in actual research projects your data does not arrive in your R script as hand-typed vectors; it arrives as a file on your computer, exported from a survey platform, an experimental software, a spreadsheet a collaborator sent you, or a database. Before you can analyze it, you have to load it into R.
This section covers the most common cases: comma-separated values (CSV) files, Excel files, and the point-and-click import feature in RStudio. We then return to the same comparison the rest of Section 1 has been building toward: code-based imports versus click-based imports, and why the code-based approach is the one to make your default.
For all the examples below, we assume you are working inside an R project (Chapter 4), so that the working directory is set to the project folder and you can refer to data files by paths relative to that folder. A common convention is to place data files in a subfolder called data inside the project, so that paths look like "data/survey_2024.csv".

7.4.1 Reading CSV files
A CSV file is a plain-text file in which rows of a table are stored as lines, and columns are separated by commas. CSV is the most common format for sharing tabular data because it is human-readable, software-agnostic, and supported by every statistical tool.
Base R has the function read.csv() for this:

survey <- read.csv("data/survey_2024.csv")

After this line, survey is a data frame with the contents of the file. You can inspect it with head(survey), str(survey), or summary(survey) as introduced in Chapter 5.
Three practical points about CSV files.
The first point is the separator. The “C” in CSV stands for “comma,” but in many European locales (including Austria, Germany, France) the convention is to use a semicolon instead, because the comma is already used as the decimal separator. If you open a CSV with read.csv() and the entire file ends up in a single column, the separator is probably a semicolon. Use read.csv2() instead, which assumes semicolon separators and comma decimals:

survey <- read.csv2("data/survey_2024.csv")

Or pass the separator explicitly to read.csv():

survey <- read.csv("data/survey_2024.csv", sep = ";", dec = ",")

The second point is the header row. By default, read.csv() assumes the first line of the file contains the column names. If your file has no header row, set header = FALSE.
The third point is alternatives in packages. The readr package (part of the tidyverse) provides read_csv(), which is faster on large files and gives clearer messages about how each column was interpreted. It returns a slightly different object (a “tibble,” which is a data frame with a few cosmetic differences). For Section 1 the base R read.csv() is sufficient.


7.4.2 Reading Excel files
Excel files have the extension .xlsx (modern Excel) or .xls (older Excel). Base R does not include a function to read them, so you need a package. The standard choice is readxl:

install.packages("readxl")  # only once, per computer
library(readxl)

survey <- read_excel("data/survey_2024.xlsx")

read_excel() handles both .xlsx and .xls. By default it reads the first sheet of the workbook. To read a specific sheet:

survey <- read_excel("data/survey_2024.xlsx", sheet = "responses")

The argument sheet accepts either the sheet name as a string or its position as a number (sheet = 2 for the second sheet).
Two notes worth flagging.
First, Excel files often contain things that do not translate well to a data frame: merged cells, formatting, formulas, multiple tables on one sheet, headers spanning several rows. If your Excel file is structured cleanly (one table per sheet, one header row, one variable per column), read_excel() works without further argument. If it is not, you may need to use range = "A3:F50" or similar to specify which cells to read. When you have control over the file, exporting it as a CSV first usually saves time.
Second, readxl reads from Excel files without needing Excel installed. The package parses the file format directly. This is a real advantage on machines that do not have Microsoft Office.


7.4.3 Point-and-click import in RStudio
RStudio includes a graphical import feature that handles both CSV and Excel files. To use it, click in the Files panel on the file you want to import, or go to File > Import Dataset in the menu and choose “From Text (base),” “From Text (readr),” or “From Excel.”
A dialog opens. It shows a preview of the data, lets you adjust options (delimiter, decimal separator, sheet for Excel files, header row, column types), and previews the result.
This is genuinely useful for one important reason: at the bottom of the dialog there is a Code Preview box that shows the R code corresponding to your current settings. Once you have the preview looking right, you can copy that code and paste it into your script.
If you simply click “Import,” the code runs once and the data appears, but the code is not added to your script. You will not be able to reproduce the import without going through the dialog again. The good practice is to use the dialog as a way to generate the code, copy it into your script, and then close the dialog.


7.4.4 Why coding the import is better
The reason to put the import in your script is the same reason to put any other step in your script. We have made this argument repeatedly in Section 1; in the context of data import it has four specific consequences.
The first is reproducibility. The import is the very first step of any analysis. If the import is in your script, then re-running the script from a clean session loads the data automatically; you do not need to remember which menu options you chose. If the import is not in your script, then your analysis is not reproducible: a colleague running your script will get an error on the very first line, because their environment does not contain the data.
The second is transparency. Reading read.csv("data/survey_2024.csv") tells the reader exactly which file is being loaded, with which separator, with which decimal convention. A click-through history tells nobody anything.
The third is portability. A scripted import using a relative path ("data/survey_2024.csv", not "C:/Users/yourname/Downloads/.../survey_2024.csv") works on any computer that has the project folder. You can email the project folder to a collaborator, or push it to a repository, and the same script will run.
The fourth is error correction. If the file’s structure changes (a new column is added, a separator changes, the file is renamed), you adjust one line of code. With a click-through workflow, you redo the entire dialog walkthrough, hoping to remember every setting you previously chose.
Use the import dialog as a helper that produces the code, then keep the code. The dialog is a good way to discover the right arguments for an unfamiliar file format; it is not a substitute for the script.


7.4.5 A practical pattern
A typical first script in a project loads the data, inspects it, and assigns it to a clean object. For example:

library(readxl)

# Load the raw data
survey <- read_excel("data/survey_2024.xlsx", sheet = "responses")

# Inspect
str(survey)
head(survey)
summary(survey)

You now have everything you need to begin analyzing real data, and you have a script that any future reader (yourself, a collaborator, a reviewer) can run from start to finish.

title: 7  Recap and getting data into R
text:
7.5 Check your understanding
1. Which best describes the relationship between R and RStudio?

 R is the engine that performs computations; RStudio is a dashboard providing a working environment around it. RStudio includes its own copy of R, so installing R separately is unnecessary. R and RStudio are the same program, just with different names. RStudio is a paid add-on that performs the statistics, while R only provides the user interface.

2. Which file type is the authoritative record of an analysis?

 An R project, because it stores objects on disk. An R script, because it is the complete written record of every step of the analysis. An RData file, because it preserves the entire environment. The Environment panel in RStudio.

3. Why is restarting the R session a recommended habit?

 It saves the environment to disk in case of a crash. It reinstalls all loaded packages from CRAN. It clears the environment and unloads packages, ensuring that running the script from the top depends only on the script itself, not on accumulated session state. It is a slow operation that should only be performed at the end of the day.

4. How often do you need to call library(packagename)?

 Once: the package is permanently active on your computer. Every R session in which you want to use the package's functions. Never: install.packages() already loads the package. Only when the package's authors release a new version.

5. Which expression extracts the column age from a data frame called survey?

 survey[age] survey$age survey.age survey->age

6. At what position is the first element of a vector in R?

 Position 0: R indexes from zero. Position 1: R indexes from one. Position -1: R indexes from the end backwards. It depends on whether the vector is numeric or character.

7. If x is a numeric vector containing one NA, what does mean(x) return?

 The mean of the entire vector regardless of NA. NA, because at least one value is missing; you would need na.rm = TRUE to compute the mean of the non-missing values. An error message that stops execution. Zero, by convention.

8. What is the main practical benefit of writing a custom function and applying it to many variables at once, rather than performing the operation manually on each variable?

 Faster computation. Automatic generation of APA-formatted output. It scales to large numbers of variables, makes the operation defined in one place easy to correct, and keeps the intent of the code transparent. It produces graphical menus for the analysis.

9. Which base R function reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file into a data frame?

 load.csv() import.csv() read.csv() open.csv()

10. You receive a CSV file from a European colleague. When you open it with read.csv(), the entire file ends up in a single column. What is the most likely cause and fix?

 Use read.csv() with no extra arguments and trust R to detect the format. Use read.csv2(), or pass sep = ";" and dec = "," to read.csv(). Convert the file to JSON before importing. Open the file in Excel and re-save it; nothing else can be done.

11. What is the recommended way to use RStudio’s “Import Dataset” dialog?

 It is faster than coding the import. It is the only way to read Excel files in R. Clicking 'Import' loads the data once, but the code is not added to your script, so the import is not reproducible. The good practice is to use the dialog to generate code, then copy that code into your script. The dialog cannot read CSV files, only Excel files.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.1 Overview
Section 1 ended with you loading a real data file into R with read.csv(). The result was a data frame, and you saw how to inspect it (head, str, summary, nrow, ncol). What you have not yet done is manipulate the data: pull out specific columns, filter rows that meet a condition, create derived variables, or compute summaries for subgroups.
This chapter covers those operations. Together they are usually called data wrangling: the work of turning a raw data file into the specific subsets and summaries you need to actually answer a research question. Good data wrangling is the foundation for everything that follows. Most of the time you spend on a real analysis is spent here, not on the statistical model itself.
We will work with one dataset throughout the chapter, and continue to use it in the chapters that follow.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.2 The example dataset
The dataset is called vgames_study.csv. It comes from a (fictional) study on the relationship between video-game playing habits and self-reported aggression. It has 120 participants and eight variables.








Variable
Type
Meaning




participant_id
integer
Unique participant identifier (1 to 120)


age
integer
Participant age in years


gender
character
Self-reported gender (man, woman, non-binary)


condition
character
Experimental condition (violent or neutral video game)


hours_weekly
numeric
Self-reported hours per week spent playing video games


trait_hostility
numeric
Score on a hostility trait scale, 1 to 7


empathy
numeric
Score on an empathy scale, 1 to 7


aggression
numeric
Self-reported aggression after the experimental session, 1 to 10



The design is a between-participants experiment: 60 participants were randomly assigned to play a violent video game and 60 to play a neutral video game. After the session, all 120 reported their aggression. The other variables (age, gender, hours of weekly play, trait hostility, empathy) were measured before the experiment.
This dataset is small and clean, which keeps the examples readable. The wrangling operations you will learn on it are exactly the same as on a real dataset of any size.

8.2.1 Getting the dataset
Download the file from https://y45hv1n.github.io/intro-data-analysis/data/vgames_study.csv and place it inside a folder called data in your R project. The path you will read from will then be "data/vgames_study.csv".
If you have not yet created an R project for this book, do that first (review Chapter 3 if you need to). For everything that follows, we assume you are inside an R project and that the file lives at data/vgames_study.csv.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.3 Loading the data
Inside your R project, in a new script, load the data and take a quick look:

data <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")

head(data)
str(data)

head(data) prints the first six rows. str(data) prints a structural summary: 120 observations, 8 variables, the type of each variable. You should see participant_id, age, and hours_weekly as numeric, and gender and condition as character (text).
The object data is now in your environment and you can refer to it by name.
A note on the object name. Calling the object data is convenient and harmless in this chapter, but data is also the name of a base R function (?data). For larger projects, a more descriptive name is better, for example vgames or study. We use data here because it matches the homework conventions you may already have seen.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
section: 8.4 Accessing one variable: the dollar sign $
text:
8.4 Accessing one variable: the dollar sign $
Chapter 5 introduced the dollar sign $ as the operator that pulls one component out of a composite object. On a data frame, $ extracts a single column. The general form is dataframe$column_name.

data$aggression
data$age
data$condition

Each of these prints an entire column as a vector. data$aggression is a numeric vector of 120 aggression scores; data$condition is a character vector of 120 condition labels.
Once you have a vector, you can do anything to it that you would do to any other vector. For example, the average aggression score across all 120 participants:

mean(data$aggression)

The expression is read inside-out: data$aggression produces a vector of 120 numbers, and mean() reduces that vector to a single number. The same inside-out logic applies whenever a function is called on a column.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.5 Creating new variables
You can add a new column to a data frame by assigning into a name that does not yet exist on the right of $:

data$aggression_doubled <- data$aggression * 2

After this line, data has nine variables instead of eight. The new column aggression_doubled contains every aggression score multiplied by two. Look at the Environment panel: the description of data should now read 120 obs. of 9 variables.
A more useful example. Compute each participant’s deviation from the mean aggression score. The mean is a single number; subtracting it from each value gives, for each participant, how far above or below the average they scored.

data$aggression_deviation <- data$aggression - mean(data$aggression)

R applies the subtraction element-wise: for every row, it computes (this participant’s aggression) minus (the overall mean aggression). The result is a new column with 120 values, some positive (above the mean), some negative (below).
To inspect the new column alongside the original, select both columns:

head(data[, c("aggression", "aggression_deviation")])

This previews the next topic: subsetting columns by name. We come back to it shortly.
The general pattern is dataframe$new_column <- expression. The expression on the right can use other columns of the same data frame, scalar values, or any R operation that produces a vector of the right length. New variables defined this way persist for the rest of the session and become part of data.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
section: 8.6 Subsetting rows: filtering by a logical condition
text:
8.6 Subsetting rows: filtering by a logical condition
You will frequently want to look at only a subset of your participants: those in the violent condition, those over 25, those with high trait hostility. The general tool for this is logical subsetting.
Two-dimensional bracket indexing on a data frame uses the form dataframe[rows, columns], where leaving a slot empty means “all.” Chapter 5 introduced this with positional indices (data[1, ] for the first row, data[, 2] for the second column). For real research, you will more often select rows by a condition.
The condition uses the double-equals operator ==, which means “is equal to.” (Single = is not a comparison in R; it is used inside function calls for named arguments. Confusing the two is a common early mistake.) For each row, R checks whether the condition is TRUE or FALSE, and the subsetting keeps only the rows where it is TRUE.
To select only participants in the violent condition:

violent_group <- data[data$condition == "violent", ]
nrow(violent_group)
# returns 60

Read the bracket from left to right. The expression data$condition == "violent" returns a logical vector of length 120 (TRUE for the 60 violent-condition participants, FALSE for the 60 neutral-condition participants). The bracket then keeps only the rows where the logical vector is TRUE. The empty slot after the comma means “all columns.”
The result violent_group is a smaller data frame with 60 rows and the same 8 (or 9, if you added new variables) columns.
Other comparisons work the same way. Some you will use often:

data[data$age > 25, ]                  # all rows where age is greater than 25
data[data$age >= 25, ]                 # age greater than or equal to 25
data[data$gender == "non-binary", ]    # only non-binary participants
data[data$gender != "man", ]           # everyone except those who reported "man"
data[data$hours_weekly < 5, ]          # participants who play fewer than 5 hours weekly

The operators are the standard ones: == (equal to), != (not equal to), <, <=, >, >=. The result of any of these comparisons is a logical vector of TRUE and FALSE values, the same length as the column being compared.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.7 Subsetting columns: by name
You can also select specific columns. The general form, again, is dataframe[rows, columns]. To keep all rows but only some columns, leave the row slot empty and pass a character vector of column names in the column slot:

data_subset <- data[, c("aggression", "condition")]
head(data_subset)

c("aggression", "condition") is a character vector with two names, so the bracket returns a data frame with all 120 rows and just those two columns, in that order.
For a single column, you could write either:

data[, "aggression"]    # bracket form, returns a vector
data$aggression         # $ form, returns the same vector

Both work. The $ form is shorter and is what you will use for one-off column access. The bracket form generalizes to multiple columns, which is why it is the right tool when you want a sub-data-frame.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
section: 8.8 Combining: filter rows and select columns at once
text:
8.8 Combining: filter rows and select columns at once
Both slots of the bracket can be filled at the same time. To get only the aggression scores of the violent-condition participants:

violent_aggression <- data[data$condition == "violent", "aggression"]
violent_aggression

The first slot filters rows (only violent condition); the second slot selects one column (aggression). Because we asked for a single column, R returns a vector, not a data frame. violent_aggression is a numeric vector of 60 aggression scores.
This single-line idiom is one of the most useful patterns in base R for inspecting subgroups. Once you know it, many small questions about your data become one-liners.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.9 Computing summaries by group
Putting the previous two pieces together, you can now compute summary statistics separately for each subgroup of interest. The first practical question of any experiment with two conditions: do the two conditions differ on the outcome?

mean(data[data$condition == "violent", "aggression"])
# returns 5.558333

mean(data[data$condition == "neutral", "aggression"])
# returns 4.213333

Two lines. Two numbers. The participants who played the violent game reported, on average, an aggression score of about 5.56; those who played the neutral game reported about 4.21. The violent-condition mean is higher by roughly 1.35 points on the 1-to-10 scale.
You can do the same with any other summary function (sd, median, min, max) and any other grouping variable. For example, the mean weekly playing hours separately by gender:

mean(data[data$gender == "man", "hours_weekly"])
mean(data[data$gender == "woman", "hours_weekly"])
mean(data[data$gender == "non-binary", "hours_weekly"])

If your dataset has many groups, this approach becomes repetitive and you will eventually want a function that does it for you in one line (we will introduce one in a later chapter). For two or three groups, the pattern above is short, transparent, and entirely sufficient.

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
section: 8.10 Looking ahead: the mean as a model
text:
8.10 Looking ahead: the mean as a model
Let us pause on what you just did. With two means, you summarized the responses of 120 people. Each of those participants is unique: a particular age, a particular hostility score, a particular history with video games. Those individual differences disappear into a single number. The mean tells you the typical aggression score for each condition, but it tells you nothing about the spread of scores within each condition, nothing about the shape of the distribution, and nothing about how individual participants varied.
That tradeoff is general. Whenever you summarize a group of people with a single number, you compress information; whatever that number does not capture is lost (at least temporarily). The art of statistical analysis is choosing summaries that capture what you actually want to know, and being explicit about what they leave out.
In the chapters that follow, we will treat the mean not as a number but as the simplest possible model of a dataset: a guess about each individual that is the same for everyone. Real models will use information about each participant (their condition, their age, their hostility) to make better, more individualized guesses. The starting point is always the mean, and the question is always: how much better can we do than the mean?

title: 8  Data wrangling: basics
text:
8.11 Check your understanding
1. What does data$aggression do?

 It is the position-based index of the column. It extracts a single named column from the data frame as a vector. It declares a new data frame. It loads a column from a CSV file.

2. What does data$aggression_doubled <- data$aggression * 2 do, assuming aggression_doubled did not previously exist in data?

 It changes the name of the column aggression in place. It produces an error because aggression_doubled does not exist yet. It creates a new column called aggression_doubled in data, containing each aggression score multiplied by two. It removes the original aggression column from data.

3. Which operator do you use inside [ ] to test whether a value is equal to another value (e.g., to filter rows where condition is "violent")?

 = (single equals). == (double equals). :=. equal().

4. What does the expression data[data$condition == "violent", ] return?

 It returns the logical vector of length 120 used inside the bracket. It returns the entire data data frame unchanged. It returns a data frame with only the rows where the condition data$condition == "violent" is TRUE, and all columns. It returns a data frame with one column called "violent".

5. What does the expression data[, c("aggression", "condition")] return?

 A character vector of values from the aggression column. A data frame with all 120 rows and only the two named columns, aggression and condition. A single number summarizing both columns. An error: you cannot select two columns at once.

6. What does the expression data[data$condition == "violent", "aggression"] return?

 A data frame of 60 rows and all columns. A numeric vector of length 60, containing the aggression scores of the 60 participants in the violent condition. A single number, the mean aggression of the violent condition. A logical vector of length 120.

7. You computed the mean aggression score for each of the two conditions and reported the two numbers. What is the most important thing those two numbers do not tell you?

 It saves a great deal of typing for an analysis that has only one or two groups. It is more accurate than computing the mean of the whole dataset. It compresses 120 individual scores into a single number per group; what the number does not encode (such as spread, shape, individual differences) is lost. It guarantees that the difference between groups is statistically significant.

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.1 Overview
Chapter 8 used base R for data wrangling: data$column to access a column, data[rows, columns] to subset, data$new <- expression to create a variable. Those operations work, and you should be comfortable reading them. They are also, for any analysis longer than a few lines, harder to read and write than the alternative we introduce here.
This chapter introduces the tidyverse, a collection of R packages designed around a consistent, readable style for data manipulation. We will learn the core operations (selecting columns, filtering rows, creating variables, sorting, grouping, summarizing, reshaping). The chapter then turns to descriptive statistics, both with base R and with the psych package, and ends with a small but important computation that connects what you have learned so far to the linear models that will appear in the rest of the book.
We continue to use vgames_study.csv as the running dataset. If you do not have it loaded, the line is data <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv").
crumbs: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.2 The tidyverse
The tidyverse is a set of R packages that share a common design philosophy and work cleanly together. The most important members for our purposes are:

dplyr, for data manipulation (selecting, filtering, summarizing).
tidyr, for reshaping data (wide to long and back).
ggplot2, for visualization (the next chapter).

When you load the tidyverse, you load all of these (and several others) at once. Install once and load every session:

install.packages("tidyverse")    # one time, per computer
library(tidyverse)               # every session

Then load the dataset:

data <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")

The rest of the chapter assumes both lines have run.
crumbs: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.3 The pipe operator
The first piece of new syntax is the pipe operator, written |>. It takes the output of one operation and passes it as the input to the next. Read it aloud as “and then.”
Without the pipe:

head(data)

With the pipe:

data |> head()

Both produce the same result: the first six rows of data. The pipe says “take data, and then apply head() to it.” For a single function call the pipe saves nothing; its value appears when you chain several operations together. We will see chaining shortly.
A note on syntax. You will sometimes see %>% in older code. It comes from a package called magrittr and behaves almost identically to |> for everyday use. The |> form is built into modern R (since R 4.1, 2021) and is the form we use. Either is fine; do not be surprised by %>% in code you read elsewhere.
crumbs: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.4 select(): choosing columns
select() keeps the columns you name and drops the rest:

data |> select(participant_id, condition, aggression)

The result is a smaller data frame with only those three columns, in that order. To keep everything except a column, prefix its name with a minus sign:

data |> select(-age)

select() returns a new data frame. It does not modify data unless you assign the result back. To save the result for later use:

data_small <- data |> select(participant_id, condition, trait_hostility, aggression)
head(data_small)
crumbs: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.5 filter(): choosing rows
filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition. The conditions use the same comparison operators introduced in Chapter 8 (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=):

data |> filter(condition == "violent")

This returns the 60 rows where condition equals "violent". Multiple conditions separated by commas are combined with “and”:

data |> filter(condition == "violent", age > 20)

Returns participants who are both in the violent condition and older than 20.
For an explicit “or,” use the vertical bar |:

data |> filter(condition == "violent" | age > 20)

A common idiom: nrow() after a filter, to count how many rows match a condition:

data |> filter(aggression > 6) |> nrow()

text:
9.6 mutate(): creating or modifying variables
mutate() adds new columns or modifies existing ones. The general form is mutate(new_name = expression):

data |> mutate(aggression_centered = aggression - mean(aggression))

This produces a data frame that is just like data except for an additional column, aggression_centered, containing each aggression score minus the mean.
mutate(), like all dplyr verbs, returns a modified copy and does not change the original unless you assign the result:

# This only prints the modified data; data itself is unchanged:
data |> mutate(aggression_centered = aggression - mean(aggression))

# This saves the modification back into data:
data <- data |> mutate(aggression_centered = aggression - mean(aggression))

This distinction is the most common source of confusion for tidyverse beginners. If you compute something and the next line does not see your new column, the most likely reason is that you forgot to assign the result.
You can also use mutate() to create logical (TRUE/FALSE) variables. The expression trait_hostility > 4 produces a logical value for each row, which mutate() stores as a new column:

data <- data |> mutate(hostility_high = trait_hostility > 4)

After this line, data has a new column hostility_high that is TRUE for participants whose trait hostility is above 4 and FALSE otherwise.

9.7 rename(): renaming variables
rename() changes column names. The syntax is new_name = old_name:

data |> rename(gaming_hours = hours_weekly)

Multiple renames in one call are separated by commas:

data_renamed <- data |> rename(hostility = trait_hostility, id = participant_id)

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.8 arrange(): sorting rows
arrange() sorts the rows of a data frame:

data |> arrange(aggression)        # lowest to highest
data |> arrange(desc(aggression))  # highest to lowest

desc() (for “descending”) wraps the column when you want the highest values first. Combine with head() to peek at the top rows:

data |> arrange(desc(trait_hostility)) |> head(1)

Returns the single most hostile participant in the dataset.

9.11 Reshaping data: long and wide format
A dataset can be in wide format or long format. Our vgames_study.csv is in wide format: each participant occupies a single row, and different measurements (age, aggression, empathy, and so on) are in different columns. Long format is the alternative: each measurement occupies a row, and a label column says which measurement it is. A participant with three measured variables would have three rows in long format.
Many statistical operations and many plots in ggplot2 expect data in long format. Converting between the two shapes is therefore a routine task.
To go from wide to long, use pivot_longer():

data_long <- data |>
  select(participant_id, aggression, empathy, trait_hostility) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(aggression, empathy, trait_hostility),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "score"
  )

head(data_long, 9)

cols lists the columns to pivot; names_to is the name of the new column that will hold the original column names; values_to is the name of the new column that will hold the values. After the pivot, each participant has three rows (one per measure) and the table has 360 rows in total (120 participants times 3 measures).
To go back, use pivot_wider():

data_wide <- data_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = measure,
    values_from = score
  )

For now, what matters is recognizing the two shapes and knowing the names of the two functions. We will return to long format when we get to plotting in the next chapter.

9.12 Descriptive statistics in base R: a brief recap
You met most of the base R summary functions in Chapter 6. To recap, on a numeric vector:

mean(data$aggression)       # arithmetic mean
median(data$aggression)     # median
sd(data$aggression)         # standard deviation
var(data$aggression)        # variance (= sd^2)
min(data$aggression)        # minimum
max(data$aggression)        # maximum
range(data$aggression)      # both, returned as a length-2 vector
sum(data$aggression)        # sum
length(data$aggression)     # number of values

For categorical variables, table() gives a frequency count:

table(data$condition)
table(data$gender)
table(data$condition, data$gender)   # cross-tabulation

These are useful when you want a quick number or two and do not need a more elaborate output.

9.13 The psych package: describe() and describeBy()
For a thorough numerical overview of every numeric variable in a data frame at once, the psych package’s describe() function is fast and complete:

library(psych)

describe(data)

For each numeric column, the output reports the count of valid values, the mean, the standard deviation, the median, the minimum, the maximum, the range, the skewness, the kurtosis, and the standard error of the mean. For research in psychology and the social sciences, this is usually exactly the set of descriptives you want for a methods or results section.
describeBy() is the same idea, but split by a grouping variable:

describeBy(data$aggression, group = data$condition)

This returns the full describe output for each level of condition, one block per group.

section: 9.15 Looking deeper: residuals from the mean
text:
9.15 Looking deeper: residuals from the mean
We end the chapter with a short computation that builds on the “mean as a model” framing introduced in Chapter 8 and previews the rest of the book.
The idea is this. The simplest possible model of a dataset is a single number: the grand mean, which is just the mean across all observations. If you had to predict the aggression score of any one participant without knowing anything else about them, the grand mean is the prediction that minimizes the total squared error. It is not a great prediction, but it is the best you can do with no information.
The error this model makes for a given participant is called a residual: the actual score minus the model’s prediction.

grand_mean <- mean(data$aggression)
grand_mean
# approximately 4.89

data <- data |> mutate(residual = aggression - grand_mean)

Each row of data now has a residual column: positive for participants who scored above the grand mean, negative for those who scored below. The sum of all residuals is approximately zero (a property of the mean: it is the value that makes the residuals balance out).

sum(data$residual)
# very close to 0, e.g. 1.42e-14

A useful summary of the model’s overall error is the sum of squared residuals, often written SS:

SS_grand <- sum(data$residual^2)
SS_grand
# approximately 307

Squaring the residuals makes them all non-negative (so positive and negative errors do not cancel) and gives more weight to large errors than to small ones. SS is the total squared error of the grand-mean model.
Now consider a slightly less naive model: instead of one prediction for everyone, one prediction per condition. The prediction for any participant is the mean aggression of their condition. To compute this, we use group_by() followed by mutate() (not summarize(), because we want to add the group mean as a column, not collapse the data to one row per group):

data <- data |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  mutate(group_mean = mean(aggression)) |>
  ungroup()

The pattern group_by() + mutate() + ungroup() is worth remembering: it adds a per-group statistic as a new column without changing the number of rows. ungroup() at the end removes the grouping so subsequent operations are not silently grouped.
Now compute residuals from this richer model and the corresponding SS:

data <- data |> mutate(residual_group = aggression - group_mean)

SS_group <- sum(data$residual_group^2)
SS_group
# approximately 245

Compare:

SS_grand
# 307
SS_group
# 245
SS_grand - SS_group
# 62

SS_group is smaller. Always. Knowing which condition a participant was in is at least as good a predictor as ignoring it, and in this dataset it is meaningfully better: the total squared error is reduced by about 62.
That difference (62, in our case) is the squared error explained by knowing the condition. It is the additional information that the group-means model captures and the grand-mean model misses. Expressed as a proportion of the original error:

(SS_grand - SS_group) / SS_grand
# approximately 0.20

About 20 percent of the variability in aggression is accounted for by knowing which condition a participant was in. The remaining 80 percent is variability within conditions: differences between participants who were in the same condition, which the group-mean model cannot explain.
This decomposition (total error = error explained by the model + error left over) is the foundation of every linear-model analysis you will see in the rest of this book. ANOVA partitions exactly this decomposition. Regression generalizes it. R-squared in any of these methods is exactly the proportion you just computed. The mean is the simplest model, group means are the next step, and the rest is more sophisticated ways of using more information about each participant to make better predictions and explain more of the variance.
You do not need to remember any of this in detail right now. What matters at this point is the workflow you used to get here: load data, wrangle it with dplyr, summarize it with summarize() or psych::describe(), and compute simple model quantities (means, residuals, sums of squares) using exactly the verbs you have just learned.

title: 9  Wrangling and describing data with the tidyverse
text:
9.16 Check your understanding
1. What does the pipe operator |> do?

 It assigns a value to a variable. It passes the output of one operation as the input to the next, so that data |> head() is equivalent to head(data). It joins two data frames together. It checks whether two values are equal.

2. Which expression keeps only the columns age and gender from data?

 data |> drop(age, gender) data |> remove(age, gender) data |> select(age, gender) data |> filter(age, gender)

3. Which expression keeps only the rows where condition is "violent"?

 data |> select(condition == "violent") data |> arrange(condition == "violent") data |> filter(condition == "violent") data |> mutate(condition == "violent")

4. What does data |> mutate(aggression_centered = aggression - mean(aggression)) do?

 It modifies the original data object in place; reassignment is not needed. It returns a new data frame with the additional column; if you want the change to persist, you must assign the result back, e.g. data <- data |> mutate(...). It deletes the column aggression from data. It throws an error if aggression_centered does not already exist.

5. What does the following pipeline return?
data |> group_by(condition) |> summarize(mean_aggression = mean(aggression), n = n())

 It returns the original data frame with one extra row containing the mean. It returns a small table with one row per condition, containing the mean aggression and the count for each condition. It returns a numeric vector of two means. It modifies data in place by adding a column called mean_aggression.

6. What is the difference between wide format and long format?

 Wide format puts every observation in its own row; long format puts every participant in its own row. Long format is for plots; wide format is for analyses. In wide format, each participant is one row and different measurements occupy different columns. In long format, each measurement is one row, and a label column identifies which measurement it is. There is no real difference; the two terms are interchangeable.

7. What does psych::describe(data) return when applied to a data frame with several numeric columns?

 Mean and standard deviation only. A row per numeric variable with n, mean, sd, median, min, max, range, skewness, kurtosis, and standard error of the mean. A bar chart of every variable. Only the names of the columns.

8. You want to add the mean aggression of each condition as a new column next to each participant’s row, without losing any rows. Which approach is correct?

 Use summarize(), which always returns one row per group. Use group_by() followed by mutate() (and then ungroup()); mutate() adds a column without collapsing the data, so per-group values appear next to each row. Use select() to choose the column. It is not possible without writing a custom function.

9. After centering a variable on its mean (x_centered = x - mean(x)), what is the sum of the centered values?

 It is undefined; the residuals can sum to anything. It is approximately zero. The mean is the value that makes the positive and negative residuals balance. It is equal to the standard deviation of the variable. It is equal to the sum of the original values.

10. You computed SS_grand (sum of squared residuals from the grand mean) and SS_group (sum of squared residuals from the per-condition means) on the same dataset. What is the relationship between the two?

 It is always larger than SS_grand. It depends on which random sample you took; sometimes larger, sometimes smaller. It is at least as small as SS_grand, and often strictly smaller. Using the group means instead of the grand mean uses more information about each participant, which reduces the total squared error. It is exactly equal to SS_grand because both models predict the same average.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.1 Overview
Up to this point we have looked at our data through numbers: counts, means, standard deviations, residuals. Numbers compress information, which is useful when you want a single value to compare or to put in a sentence. But numbers also hide information, and what they hide can change the answer to a research question.
This chapter is about the other half of looking at data: visualization. The chapter does not contain plotting code yet. The reason is deliberate: it is much easier to learn the how of plotting once you know the what and the why. We start with the questions a good plot answers, the conceptual framework that organizes every plot you will ever make, the principles that distinguish a good plot from a bad one, and the kinds of judgment calls you will face when reading or making one. The tools to translate these decisions into actual plots in R come in the next chapter.
The plots that appear throughout this chapter are produced with ggplot2, the R package you will learn in the next chapter. The code for each plot is hidden for now, so you can focus on the visual outcome rather than the syntax. You will revisit these examples and reproduce them yourself once you have learned the package.
crumbs: 10  First principles of data visualization

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.2 Why visualize?
A famous example illustrates the problem with relying on summary statistics alone. Anscombe’s quartet is a set of four small datasets, constructed by the statistician Frank Anscombe in 1973, that have nearly identical summary statistics. The quartet is built into R, so you can inspect it directly:

data("anscombe")
anscombe

The data frame has eight columns: four x columns (x1, x2, x3, x4) and four corresponding y columns (y1, y2, y3, y4). Each (x, y) pair is one of the four datasets. Each dataset has 11 observations.
Compute the means of all eight columns:

sapply(anscombe, mean)
# x1 x2 x3 x4   y1   y2   y3   y4
#  9  9  9  9 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50

All four x means are 9.0 and all four y means are 7.50. The four standard deviations agree to two decimals as well, and the four correlation coefficients between x and y are all approximately 0.82. If you compute the line of best fit (the regression line) for each pair, all four lines are essentially the same.
By every numerical summary you can think of at this point, the four datasets are interchangeable.
When you plot them, they look completely different.









Dataset 1 is a clean, roughly linear relationship. Dataset 2 is a smooth curve where a straight line is the wrong model entirely. Dataset 3 is a near-perfect linear relationship plus one extreme outlier that pulls the regression line away from the true pattern. Dataset 4 is a vertical line of constant x with one isolated point at a very different x; that single point is what creates the apparent correlation.
Four datasets, four very different stories, identical summary statistics. The lesson Anscombe drew, and the one this book takes seriously, is short: always plot your data. Numerical summaries do not protect you from misreading what is actually in the dataset.
A good visualization does things that numbers alone cannot:

It reveals the shape of a distribution (symmetric? skewed? bimodal?).
It shows the relationship between variables (linear? curved? no pattern?).
It exposes outliers and unusual observations.
It communicates findings to others quickly and intuitively, in a way that a table of numbers cannot.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.3 The grammar of graphics
Most modern data-visualization systems (including ggplot2, the R package you will learn in the next chapter) are based on a framework called the grammar of graphics, formalized by the statistician Leland Wilkinson. The core idea is that any plot is built from the same three ingredients, combined in different ways.









Data. The dataset you want to visualize. Without data there is nothing to plot. The data are usually a data frame.
Aesthetics. A mapping from variables in the data to visual properties of the plot. Examples: the x-axis represents hours_weekly; the y-axis represents aggression; the color of each point represents condition; the size of each point represents age. Each aesthetic mapping turns one variable into one visual channel.
Geometry. The visual shape used to represent each observation. Examples: points (a scatterplot), bars (a bar chart), lines (a line chart), boxes (a boxplot), tiles (a heatmap).
By choosing data, aesthetics, and a geometry, you specify the plot. The grammar is called a “grammar” by analogy with language: just as a finite vocabulary plus a set of rules generates an unbounded number of sentences, a finite set of aesthetics and geometries plus a dataset generates an unbounded number of plots.
This vocabulary will become concrete the moment you write your first ggplot2 line. The point of introducing it now is that plots are not arbitrary collections of marks on a page. They are the result of three explicit decisions, and you can usually improve a bad plot by going back and rethinking one of the three.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
section: 10.4 Seven principles of good data visualization
text:
10.4 Seven principles of good data visualization
Reasonable people disagree about details, but the field has converged on a small set of principles. The seven that follow are the most consequential for the kinds of plots you will make as a researcher. We state each one as a directive and then explain it.

10.4.1 1. Show the data, not just summaries
A bar chart that displays only the group means is a bar chart that hides the individual observations. The reader cannot tell whether the difference between groups reflects a consistent difference across all participants or a small number of extreme participants pulling the mean in one direction. Whenever possible, show the individual data points (for example, as a scatter or jittered dots) in addition to any summary statistic, or use a geometry like a boxplot or violin plot that displays the distribution rather than collapsing it to a single number.
Bad example. A bar chart of group means, with no indication of within-group variability or individual scores.









Good example. The same group means, with all individual scores overlaid as jittered points. Now the reader sees the spread within each group and can judge whether the difference in means reflects a consistent shift or a few extreme scores.











10.4.2 2. Choose the right geometry for the data type
The right geometry depends on what kind of variables you have:

One continuous variable, distribution. Use a histogram or a density plot. These show the shape of the distribution: where it is centered, how spread out it is, whether it is symmetric or skewed, whether it has a single peak or multiple peaks.
One categorical variable, counts. Use a bar chart. Each bar represents a category; the bar height represents the count or proportion in that category.
Two continuous variables, relationship. Use a scatterplot. Each observation is one point; the relationship between the variables (linear, curved, none) becomes visible at a glance.
One continuous variable across one categorical variable, group comparison. Use a boxplot, a violin plot, or overlaid histograms. These show how the distribution of the continuous variable differs across groups.

There are more advanced choices for more complicated questions, but the four above cover most of what you will plot.
Bad example. A bar chart used to display the relationship between two continuous variables (hours_weekly and aggression). Bar charts are designed for categorical comparisons; using one here forces a continuous variable into discrete bars and discards the relationship.









Good example. A scatterplot. Each participant is one point; the relationship (or absence of one) is visible directly.











10.4.3 3. Label everything clearly
Every axis needs a label. The label should describe the variable in plain language (“Aggression Score (1-10)”), not the column name from the dataset (aggression). If you use color or shape to encode a variable, include a legend that explains what each color or shape means. Give the plot a title that states what it shows. A reader who sees the plot for the first time, with no other context, should be able to identify what is being shown.
Bad example. A scatterplot with no title, default axis labels (the raw column names), and no legend explanation. A reader without context cannot tell what is being shown.









Good example. Same plot with a descriptive title, plain-language axis labels, and a legend identifying the conditions.











10.4.4 4. Avoid chart junk
The term chart junk was popularized by the statistician Edward Tufte. It refers to visual elements that do not encode information: unnecessary gridlines, 3D effects on a 2D plot, decorative images, drop shadows, gradient fills, excessive colors. Chart junk distracts the reader from the actual data and signals carelessness. Every element on a plot should serve a purpose. If you can remove an element without losing information, remove it.
Bad example. The same data, encrusted with chart junk: gradient bars, dark gridlines, heavy borders, oversaturated colors.









Good example. Same data, with everything that does not encode information removed. The bars are the only visual element with weight; the eye goes directly to the comparison.











10.4.5 5. Do not mislead with scales
The scale of an axis controls how big a difference looks on the page. A small difference in y-values can be made to look enormous by truncating the y-axis to start near the data values rather than at zero. The classic example: bars that visually look twice as tall but actually differ by 0.1 on a scale of 1 to 10, because the y-axis has been truncated to range from 4.0 to 6.0 instead of 0 to 10. This is misleading and you should not do it.
Two related rules. Do not use dual y-axes. A plot with two different y-axes (one on the left, one on the right) almost always misleads, because the reader cannot tell which line corresponds to which axis without effort, and the apparent relationship between the lines depends entirely on how the two axes are scaled. Use consistent scales when comparing plots. If you show two plots side by side, the reader will compare them visually; using different scales for the same variable will mislead.
Bad example. The y-axis is truncated to range from 4.0 to 6.0. The two bars look dramatically different in height; the visual impression is that the violent condition produced an enormous effect.









Good example. Same data, y-axis on its natural scale (1 to 10). The difference between conditions is real and interpretable, but it is not visually inflated.











10.4.6 6. Avoid pie charts
Pie charts ask the reader to compare the angles of slices, and humans are demonstrably bad at comparing angles. Comparing the heights of bars is much easier and more accurate. Almost every situation in which someone reaches for a pie chart is better served by a bar chart. There are a few special cases (a pie with two or three slices when the goal is to communicate “this small slice versus everything else”), but the default should be a bar chart.
Bad example. A pie chart of gender counts. Comparing slices by angle is harder than reading bar heights.









Good example. Same data as a bar chart. The differences in counts are immediate.











10.4.7 7. Use color purposefully
Color in a plot should encode information, not decorate it. Each distinct color should mean something specific (one experimental condition, one category of participants, one variable). Use a small number of colors; a plot with ten colors is a plot the reader cannot interpret.
A practical detail: roughly 8 percent of men and 0.5 percent of women have some form of color-vision deficiency, most commonly red-green confusion. Plots that distinguish groups by red versus green are unreadable for those readers. Use color palettes designed to be colorblind-friendly (any modern plotting library, including ggplot2, provides such palettes), and where possible reinforce color with a second visual channel like shape or line type, so the plot remains interpretable even for readers who cannot distinguish the colors.
Bad example. Each participant has been given a different rainbow color for no reason. The colors do not encode anything; they are pure decoration. The reader gets no information from them and the plot is harder to read than the same plot in one color.









Good example. Color is used to encode the experimental condition (the variable the reader actually wants to compare), with a colorblind-safe palette (blue and orange).

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.5 Applying the principles
The principles are abstract; they become useful when you apply them to a specific plot. The following five short scenarios illustrate the kind of judgment a careful researcher makes when reading or designing a visualization.
Scenario 1. A researcher wants to show how aggression scores are distributed across all 120 participants. Two options: (a) a bar chart showing the mean aggression score as a single bar, or (b) a histogram showing the distribution of all 120 aggression scores. The histogram is more informative. A single bar tells you one number (the mean). The histogram shows the shape of the distribution, the spread, possible outliers, and any clustering. The bar discards 119 numbers; the histogram keeps them. Principle 1 in action.


















Scenario 2. A researcher wants to compare aggression between the violent and neutral conditions. He produces a bar chart with two bars (one per condition) showing the group means. What is missing? At least three things. The plot does not show the spread of scores within each condition (so you cannot tell whether the difference between groups is large relative to within-group variation). It does not show the individual data points (so you cannot tell whether the difference is driven by all participants or by a few extreme ones). It does not show the shape of the within-group distributions (so you cannot tell whether either group is skewed or has outliers). Better alternatives: overlay the individual data points on the bars; use a boxplot or violin plot per condition; or show the distribution as overlaid histograms. Each of these shows the data, not just the summaries.




































Scenario 3. A researcher wants to examine whether there is a relationship between weekly playing hours (a continuous variable) and aggression (a continuous variable). Which geometry is most appropriate? A scatterplot. Each participant becomes one point at the (hours_weekly, aggression) coordinates, and the relationship (positive, negative, none, linear, curved) is visible directly. A bar chart is wrong because both variables are continuous; a pie chart is wrong because the question is not about proportions; a boxplot is wrong because neither variable is categorical.




































Scenario 4. Suppose you have the same data displayed two ways: option A is a boxplot with one box per condition, with individual data points overlaid; option B is a small table reporting “Violent: M = 5.56, SD = 1.66; Neutral: M = 4.21, SD = 1.24.” Both convey the same basic information. When is the plot better, and when is the table better? The plot is better when you want to communicate to a broad audience, when you want the reader to see the distribution rather than just the summary, and when you suspect the distributions might be unusual (skewed, bimodal, with outliers) and want the reader to check that for themselves. The table is better when you need exact numbers (for reporting in a paper), when the audience is technically sophisticated and prefers precision, or when you have many groups and a plot would become cluttered. In practice, good scientific communication often uses both: a plot for pattern, a table or in-text numbers for precision.










Option B: summary table


Condition
M
SD




Violent
5.56
1.66


Neutral
4.21
1.24



Scenario 5. A researcher plots aggression on the y-axis (the variable ranges from 1 to 10) but sets the y-axis limits to 4.0 to 6.0. The bars for the two conditions now appear dramatically different in height. What is wrong with this? The truncated y-axis visually exaggerates the difference. The actual difference between the two condition means (about 1.35 points on a 1-to-10 scale) is real and worth reporting, but it is not as large as the truncated plot makes it look. The fix is to start the y-axis at the natural minimum of the scale, or at least to show enough of the range that the difference is in proper proportion. If the difference is small relative to the scale of the variable, that is itself a finding and should not be visually inflated. Principle 5 in action.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.6 The wrangle, describe, visualize workflow
You now have three skills that work together:

Data wrangling (Chapters 8 and 9): getting the data into the right shape, selecting the variables you need, filtering to the rows that are relevant, creating derived variables.
Descriptive statistics (Chapter 9): summarizing the data numerically, with summary(), mean(), psych::describe(), or a custom summarize() pipeline.
Data visualization (this chapter, conceptually; the next chapter, in code): communicating patterns visually.

The order in practice is almost always: wrangle first (clean, filter, reshape), then describe (compute summaries to check what you have), then visualize (plot what looks important). Wrangling is usually the largest time investment and the least visible step in a finished paper. Descriptives are how you sanity-check the wrangling. Visualization is how you discover what is worth modeling and how you communicate the results once you have modeled them.

title: 10  First principles of data visualization
text:
10.7 Looking ahead
The next chapter introduces ggplot2, the package that lets you implement the principles of this chapter in actual R code. ggplot2 is the visualization component of the tidyverse you loaded in Chapter 9, so you do not need to install anything new. You will see how each of the three ingredients of the grammar of graphics (data, aesthetics, geometry) becomes a piece of code, and how the same dataset can be displayed in radically different and informative ways.
For now, the principles in this chapter are the things to keep in mind. Good plots are not the result of decorative talent; they are the result of a small number of decisions made carefully.
